World.title: Australian Opals coach suspended for ‘inappropriate comment’ to star player
World.content:
SportBasketballWNBA Australian Opals coach suspended for ‘inappropriate comment’ to star player Frances Howe July 19, 2026 — 1:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian coach Sandy Brondello has been given a one-game suspension for calling an opposing player a “protected species” during a game on Saturday (AEST). Brondello, 57, is head coach of the Opals – Australia’s women’s basketball team – and the Toronto Tempo, an expansion team in North America’s Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA). Sandy Brondello is head coach of the Australian Opals and the WNBA’s Toronto Tempo. Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The WNBA released a statement on Sunday morning (AEST) announcing that Brondello had been suspended without pay for one game for an “inappropriate comment” made about high-profile Atlanta Dream forward, Angel Reese. Brondello could be heard on the broadcast saying, “Angel, she’s a protected species” after a Tempo player, Nyara Sabally, was called for a defensive foul on Reese late in the game. Immediately after, Sabally was treated by the team’s medical staff for a rib injury and did not return to action. The Dream beat the Tempo 111-92.



The phrase “protected species” is often used in an Australian sporting context when referring to players who are thought to get preferential treatment from match officials. The comment was picked up by users on X after the game before Reese herself shared a post and tagged Brondello in it. The user had written, “Calling a black woman a species ...” To which Reese wrote, “Are we surprised!?” and added a clown emoji. Atlanta Dream’s Angel Reese shoots during a game against the Toronto Tempo in June. Getty Images Reese is one of the WNBA’s most recognisable players and is the current league leader in rebounds per game. Brondello responded with her own post, which read: “Angel, I’m sorry. Last night, in the emotion of the moment after Nyara’s injury, I used a phrase that I shouldn’t have used, and I take full responsibility for that. My frustration was with the officiating, but my words unfairly put the focus on you.



“I also understand that my words carried an impact beyond what I intended, particularly for Black women in our league, and I’m deeply sorry for that. I’ve spent my career competing with, coaching and learning from incredible Black women. “I regret that my words caused hurt to a community I respect so deeply. I have a lot of respect for you as both a player and a person, and I sincerely apologise to you, your teammates, and the Dream organisation for my comment.” View post on X The WNBA confirmed Brondello would serve the ban in the Tempo’s next match against the Las Vegas Aces on Tuesday (AEST) and added, “The WNBA expects all coaches and team personnel to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and respect that are fundamental to our league.” Brondello’s comment and ban have been made during a time of heightened concern in the league regarding the racial vilification of black players. The league’s commissioner Cathy Engelbert and its most high-profile player Caitlin Clark both made public statements earlier this month when Phoenix Mercury’s Alyssa Thomas was subjected to death threats and racial abuse online after she fouled Clark in a game on June 24.



A man was also fired from his job at a Hilton Hotel this week after calling Aces’ guard Chelsea Gray a racial slur over Instagram direct message. Related Article WNBA Why Serena Williams is this Australian’s new boss Reese did not reply to Brondello’s apology but shared another post which wrote “so many girls can learn from how [Reese] stands up for herself.” Three-time championship-winning college basketball coach and three-time Olympic gold medallist, Dawn Staley shared Brondello’s post and added “a real apology”. Brondello was announced as head coach of the Tempo for their inaugural season this year. She has coached in the WNBA since 2005 and was a player in the league before that. She is one of just two WNBA coaches to win championships with different teams and is the only Australian coach in the league.



During her time as a player for the Opals, Brondello competed at three Olympic Games – winning one bronze and two silver medals. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: The device detecting the world’s deadliest creature
World.content:
NationalNSWAI The device detecting the world’s deadliest creature Angus Dalton July 19, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To some, it’s just annoying, but to others, it marks the chilling call of the world’s deadliest creature: the buzz of a mosquito. In an effort to slash the extraordinary death toll wreaked by the insects, a University of Wollongong researcher has harnessed a super-efficient, lo-fi form of AI that can discern a disease-carrying mosquito from a harmless one by tuning in to this buzz. A low-powered AI device could help detect the world’s worst mosquito species. Michael Howard The detection device is one of a raft of new inventions using tiny machine learning, or TinyML, a low-power type of AI serving as the antithesis to the voracious large language models that require energy-guzzling data centres. First, Associate Professor Kiran Trivedi wanted to see if TinyML could identify the bird calls floating through his window.



Trivedi, a computer science expert from the university’s Indian campus in Ahmedabad, downloaded bird call data from Google and created a small model deployed onto a tiny chip that could identify the calls of species such as the Indian cuckoo. Once that was working, he turned to babies. Trivedi’s brother, a pediatrician who works in a neonatal ward, told him anxious new parents often brought in their infants to ask the doctor why they were crying. “So again, I collected the data for babies’ crying sounds, and created a model for that.” The result was another experimental device designed to deduce whether a baby was bawling because of hunger, sleepiness or discomfort.



“That is how it started,” Trivedi said. But crying babies, he thought, were hardly the world’s biggest problem. So he pivoted to mosquitoes, which kill 700,000 people per year via malaria, dengue and Zika. Each species has a unique wing beat. The malaria-carrying kind, Anopheles, has a low-pitched buzz. Culex mosquitoes carry Japanese encephalitis and Ross River virus; they buzz at medium pitch. Aedes aegypti, a dengue-carrying species also found in Australia, flies at the highest pitch. Associate Professor Kiran Trivedi at the UN’s AI for Good summit this week. UN AI for Good Trivedi used 40 gigabytes of mosquito sound data, equivalent to 10,000 stored photos, to make a model that was 150 megabytes – still too large for a small chip. To compress the model, he converted the audio recordings into images called “spectrograms”, which are visual representation of soundwaves. The AI learned to pick up patterns in the images invisible to the human eye.



Then, through a process called “quantisation”, he stripped back and simplified the model until only the information essential for making accurate predictions remained. The resulting model was a tiny 19 kilobytes, about the size of a five-page Word document. Associate Professor Kiran Trivedi’s lo-fi mosquito detection device. University of Wollongong “I deployed that onto my device, connected a display and some batteries, and it was, surprisingly, a perfectly working device.” He caught a mosquito in his room in Ahmedabad, in western India, and let it fly near the device. It was detected as an Anopheles mosquito; by far the deadliest species. The device is currently 88.3 per cent accurate.



This is TinyML at work, a form of AI that can operate off-grid, independently, on a tiny chip with little power. With the energy an LLM uses to generate a paragraph of text, a TinyML device can run for weeks. Related Article Data centres ‘More questions than answers’: Albanese’s data-centre vision risks renewables rollout “For AI, usually we need massive [amounts of] data, a powerful machine, and an internet network or Wi-Fi,” said Associate Professor Jianlong Zhou, an AI researcher at the University of Technology Sydney not involved in Trivedi’s research. “TinyML is different – we can use it in places with no power, no internet, no network. “TinyML collects data locally, processes it locally, and gives feedback locally, so there’s no privacy issues.” Zhou has researched TinyML applications in beekeeping, where TinyML nanosensors can monitor a hive’s environment down to humidity, CO2, pheromone imbalances in the queen bee, early chemical signs of Varroa mite infestations, and the vibrations of bees which signal an impending swarming event.



Smart agriculture, as well as wearable health sensors, will be major drivers of TinyML technology in the near future, he says. By one estimate, the number of TinyML devices in operation will spike to 2.5 billion by 2030. As for Trivedi’s device, he dreams the sensors could be mass-produced for 500 rupees, or about $7.50, and become part of a citywide detection network. A mock-up mosquito monitoring dashboard envisioned by Dr Kiran Trivedi, that could one day operate based on his devices. Dr Kiran Trivedi “It’s all about early detection,” he said. “Usually, what happens where I live is that you read in the newspaper that there are a lot of mosquitos breeding, and dengue has been found. But the outbreak has already happened and a lot of people have already been infected.” The technology he’s working on could catch mosquito outbreaks as they begin, leading to targeted early control measures such as insecticide fogging. He also imagines the model built into smart speakers such as Alexa and alerting people when a disease-causing mosquito is buzzing nearby.



Trivedi displayed his technology at the UN’s AI for Good summit this week. “If we can identify the mosquito species and help society, it could be a great success for me,” he said. The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: This is what English football looks like when the pressure is off
World.content:
SportFIFA World Cup This is what English football looks like when the pressure is off Mike McGrath Updated July 19, 2026 — 1:46pm ,first published 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: England played in the craziest match of the World Cup as they defeated France in a 10-goal thriller to win the bronze medal on Saturday (Sunday, AEST). At one stage, they looked like throwing away a four-goal lead at the Hard Rock Stadium, before seeing out a 6-4 win and securing their best finish at the tournament since winning in 1966. Jude Bellingham, Bukayo Saka and Reece James celebrate Saka’s hat-trick. Getty Images Here’s a look at the madness in Miami during the third-place play-off. Attacking intent



There were eyebrows raised when Declan Rice was selected despite his 68 previous games this season. He has described it as an “obscene” amount of matches but was called upon for one last effort and was charging forward in the first few minutes, intercepting a pass and curling into the bottom corner to kick off the scoring. But England were not done – there was no sitting back on their lead as they did against Argentina. England manager Thomas Tuchel’s attackers were pouring forward and getting behind the French defence with balls over the top. Ezri Konsa and Bukayo Saka (twice) were on the scoresheet by half-time. Loading The French not turning up As good as England were in that first 45 minutes, it was clear that France were already on the beach following their defeat by Spain in the semi-final earlier in the week. Players who were used to high-intensity pressing were allowing white shirts to walk past them with the ball.



By the break, Saka had run 1.4km more than Kylian Mbappe. This was Didier Deschamps’s final game in charge of Les Bleus, but players were treating it like an exhibition match. Flicks, tricks and no defending. The best half-time interview The half-time interview is another of FIFA’s new ideas. They have largely just been anodyne, aside from when Anthony Barry is in front of the camera. Tuchel’s assistant has been a breath of fresh air with his honesty and fought back the tears when analysing England’s first 45 minutes. “I am a little bit emotional, I can’t find the words to describe just how proud I am of these players,” said Barry. “They are playing a game out on the field with broken hearts, I see 11 lads out on the field with broken hearts, I’ve seen them in the hotel last few days – broken hearts.” Kylian Mbappe celebrates scoring his side’s third goal against England. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell



France go through the gears France decided to step it up after the half-time interval, with Deschamps calling for Ousmane Dembele and Bradley Barcola off the bench to lead their attack. Immediately, England were on the back foot despite being four goals up. Mbappe decided to show up too, pulling one back and celebrating with body language that suggested: we’re still in this. Barcola also found the net. This was Didier Deschamps’s final game in charge of Les Bleus, but players were treating it like an exhibition match. Mbappe takes command of Golden Boot race Mbappe’s double means he has overtaken Lionel Messi as the highest-scoring player in World Cup history, with 22. There is a question over whether goals in the third-placed play-off should count, but as it stands, they most certainly do. The Frenchman now has 10 at this tournament, two ahead of Messi – who plays in the final on Sunday.



It is the first time a player has reached double figures in one tournament since Gerd Müller for West Germany. Michael Olise set up his two goals and that made the former Crystal Palace midfielder the most creative World Cup player in the last 60 years with his seven assists. This is England’s best men’s World Cup since 1966. Getty Images England fail to learn lessons from semi-final ... This ended in victory for England, but there were red flags too with how France were allowed back in the game. Tuchel’s team dropped deep just like they did in Atlanta when they took the lead against Argentina. Tuchel says one of the big problems England face is how they play when the pressure is on. And once France started trying, they made England buckle again. ... but getting over the line



For the final 11 minutes, Tuchel called for his “starters” who had been rested on the bench. Jude Bellingham came on, to the delight of the neutral fans in attendance. Related Article FIFA World Cup Messi the link between Argentina and Spain’s colliding contrasts Elliot Anderson also came off the bench to try and keep the ball in central midfield, shifting the formation after England were in a 4-4-2. It was Djed Spence, one of England’s breakout stars of the tournament, who earned a penalty when the game was in the balance. Saka’s history-making hat-trick Bellingham has been “protecting the ball” for penalties, standing over the spot and holding the ball so opponents cannot get in the ear of England’s actual taker. He did this for Harry Kane earlier in the tournament. But with Kane rested, Saka completed his hat-trick from the penalty spot. The Arsenal forward was an unused sub against Argentina but made history with his hat-trick here, joining Geoff Hurst, Gary Lineker and Kane as England players with World Cup hat-tricks to their name.



Stoppage-time chaos Dembele set up a frantic final few minutes when he found the net, finishing off a counter-attack started by Dayot Upamecano. There was still time for Bellingham to round off his stunning cameo with a spectacular goal, running through the France defence and dummying the goalkeeper before finding the net. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Trump launches retaliatory strikes after Iran kills two US troops in Jordan
World.content:
Updated WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump launches retaliatory strikes after Iran kills two US troops in Jordan Michael Koziol Updated July 19, 2026 — 2:23pm ,first published July 19, 2026 — 4:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The United States launched a fresh wave of strikes against Iran after two American troops were killed by an Iranian attack on an air base in Jordan, representing another escalation in a war that is again engulfing the Middle East. The strikes began at 8am on Sunday (AEST) at President Donald Trump’s direction, Central Command (Centcom) said. They were designed to “swiftly punish” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for its attack, as well as to continue degrading Iran’s ability to threaten shipping. Mojtaba Khamenei (right), who was last seen before the war began, called US President Donald Trump’s (left) signature “worthless” in a statement given to Iranian state TV. Multiple explosions were heard near Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city on the Strait of Hormuz, and the nearby island of Qeshm, according to the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency. They were the eighth consecutive night of US strikes, and lasted more than five hours. Strikes hit Iran’s military coastal surveillance and air defence facilities, maritime capabilities and missile and drone storage sites, Centcom said, while also targeting IRGC forces responsible for the attack in Jordan.



Meanwhile, the US State Department issued a worldwide travel caution, advising Americans – especially those in the Middle East – of possible flight cancellations and airspace closures, and targeted attacks on US interests by Iran and its supporters. The two troops were killed in Jordan on Friday as the US and its partner forces defended against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks. Another service member is missing, while four others were medically evacuated to Jordanian hospitals and later discharged. US drones hit Bandar Abbas Naval Base earlier this week. U.S. Central Command via AP The dead were not publicly identified. Since the war began at the end of February, 16 American service members have been killed and more than 430 wounded. Trump told News Nation the deaths were “very sad” but came in service to their country. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote on X: “Godspeed, heroes. Their sacrifice only stiffens our resolve.”



A ceasefire was declared in mid-June when the US and Iran signed a memo that began a 60-day peace negotiation process. But after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired at ships in the Strait of Hormuz nearly a fortnight ago, the fighting has resumed, and the talks have collapsed. US forces have also recommenced a blockade of ships accessing Iranian ports. And Trump has weighed escalating the conflict, publicly stating that he was considering attacks on Pickaxe Mountain, a key Iranian nuclear site, or a US takeover of Kharg Island, a major oil terminal. An army cadet walks past a billboard bearing anti-Trump messages, including the phrase “we kill Trump”, in central Tehran. AP Photo/Vahid Salemi On Sunday (AEST) Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a fresh statement condemning the US and declaring that the large crowds who turned out for his father’s funeral showed “a new chapter of awakening and active engagement” was underway in Iran and Iraq. Khamenei has not been seen since the war began, but his remarks were read out on state TV and posted in English on his social media account.



“The repeated breaches of the agreement by the Great Satan [the US] regarding the MOU signed by the Presidents of Iran and the US have once again laid bare a fundamental truth: the signature of the US President is utterly worthless and devoid of credibility,” Khamenei said. “Now that the American enemy is seeking to escalate the conflict, thereby incurring even heavier costs and further humiliation, it should know that the noble nation of Iran and the Resistance Front have unforgettable lessons in store for it.” Related Article Updated

Middle East at war Iran renews attacks on Gulf states after another night of US strikes The comments came hours after a negotiator said Tehran was suspending its commitments to the interim deal signed last month. Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, told state TV that the US has violated its commitments under the deal that was signed about a month ago and now Iran is “no longer implementing them”. Trump has also declared the ceasefire agreement “over”.



Video circulating online purported to show an Iranian missile striking Jordan’s Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, where US forces have based warplanes used in its attacks against Iran. The same base was attacked earlier this week, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials. Significant damage from the latest Iranian strikes also occurred in Kuwait, where a water desalination plant and an oil facility were hit, according to the Kuwait authorities and the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation. Loading The strikes injured several people at the oil facility and caused a fire at the desalination plant, forcing several power generation units offline. It was the second attack against a desalination plant in two days in the tiny desert nation that depends on desalination for 90 per cent of its drinking water. Meanwhile, Iraq said it shot down attack drones over the city of Irbil. Jordan’s state-run Petra news agency said the kingdom’s air defence systems had downed Iranian missiles, while air sirens sounded multiple times in Bahrain throughout the day and in Saudi Arabia in the morning, according to their governments.



Iran’s renewed attacks on its Gulf neighbours, including domestic infrastructure, is a return to a hallmark of the conflict’s early stages, whereby the Islamic regime targeted America’s partners in the region following US strikes. Saudi Arabia strongly condemned Iran’s latest attacks as “violations of international law and the principles of good neighbourliness”, offered its full support for any retaliatory efforts by the countries that were hit. The secretary general of the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, Jasem Mohamed al-Budaiwi, accused Iran of war crimes for strikes on infrastructure and civilian facilities. Danny Citrinowicz, a senior Iran researcher at the Israel-based Institute for National Security Studies, said events were slipping beyond anyone’s control, and the risk of further escalation now exceeded the prospect of de-escalation. “There are no effective guardrails, the mediators are losing leverage, one side believes additional pressure will eventually weaken Iran enough to force concessions, while the other increasingly views this as an existential struggle,” he wrote on X.



The expanding scope would likely draw Gulf neighbours more directly into the conflict, putting strategic targets and critical infrastructure at risk, Citrinowicz said. “Unless something significant changes soon, this conflict is on a trajectory toward a far more dangerous phase, one that may become increasingly difficult for either side to contain.” With AP

World.title: ‘Larger than life’: Home and Away’s Terence Donovan dies aged 90
World.content:
Terence Donovan, a British-Australian actor known for his roles in TV soaps Neighbours and Home and Away, has died aged 90.

Born in London, Donovan came to Australia with his parents when he was 14. Before acting, he worked as a house painter and a truck driver. He starred in the films Breaker Morant and The Man from Snowy River, as well as TV series Division 4 and Cop Shop, before playing Doug Willis on Neighbours in more than 500 episodes

His actor and singer son, Jason Donovan, shared the news that his father had passed away on Saturday night in Melbourne, in an update to Instagram.

Terry Donovan with his sons. Instagram

“It is with great sadness but also a sense of celebration of a long, full life that myself and my brother Paul announce our father Terence died peacefully last night here in Melbourne,” the update said.

World.title: Hanson is sweating her five-star Euro summer more than she’s willing to let on
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropePauline Hanson Hanson is sweating her five-star Euro summer more than she’s willing to let on David Crowe Updated July 19, 2026 — 2:01pm ,first published 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Pauline Hanson seems more anxious about her European holiday than she cares to admit. And she has just revealed an incredible sensitivity about the questions from the media about how she ended up at a luxury fashion show in Sicily. The One Nation leader has been making headlines with her trip to a Dolce & Gabbana show in Taormina and her stay at a five-star hotel with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart, her friend and patron. Hanson and James Ashby knew reporters at CPAC would ask her questions she did not want to answer. So they ran for cover. Luca Marino She was clearly bristling at all this attention over the past few days – and went to extraordinary lengths to dodge questions after she landed in London to speak at the right-wing Conservative Political Action Conference. Hanson and her chief adviser, James Ashby, knew reporters at CPAC would ask her questions she did not want to answer. So they ran for cover. They stayed behind a VIP cordon guarded by security staff. They raced past reporters in the rare moments they were in a public space. Hanson did not take a single question.



Most of the Australian media in London were at CPAC to see Hanson speak on Saturday morning and, if all went well, ask a few questions. There were at least a dozen reporters, from every major media outlet, including this one. Pauline Hanson speaks at CPAC GB in London, in a room with rows of empty seats. Luca Marino Pauline Hanson attends the CPAC conference in London with her adviser, James Ashby (left). Luca Marino ABC reporters Elias Clure and Riley Stuart at least managed to get to Hanson when she walked past quickly at the Intercontinental Hotel at the O2 arena at Greenwich. They asked if she had paid for her time in Sicily. Her response? “I need to go inside.” Even when Hanson appeared in the audience to hear Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, she walked afterwards to the VIP area rather than going anywhere a journalist could approach. She did the same when she addressed the conference on Saturday morning. The VIP zone was her safe space.



All this hiding became faintly ludicrous. For hours after her speech, knowing journalists wanted to ask her questions, she stayed out of sight at the plush hotel. Ashby would emerge every so often to see if the coast was clear. Finally, he collected various bags from the concierge and made his way to a taxi at the front of the hotel – with Hanson nowhere in sight. The One Nation leader was clearly about to depart. The mystery was how. The cab drove off with Ashby inside. A camera operator followed some of the way on foot. Minutes later, the cab turned up again, behind where it had started. It had done a full circuit of the hotel, using an access road that skirted the vast O2 arena. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson was spotted in Italy with mining magnate Gina Rinehart. Brisbane-based luxury jeweller Margot McKinney (left) and Pauline Hanson at the Dolce & Gabbana Alta Moda fashion show in Taormina, Sicily. @beatyesterday_art The cab stopped. Ashby, on his mobile phone, leant forward to issue instructions to the driver. The cab moved off again, this time faster. It was not seen again. The taxi probably drove around to the access road, and Hanson probably left the hotel through a corridor to the O2 arena that led to the road and the taxi, which reversed and drove away.



The wait took hours. The escape took time and effort. And it only happened because Hanson is so touchy about taking questions. Related Article Updated

Political leadership ‘Do not apologise for being white’: Hanson takes aim at privilege and trans rights Here are a few she needs to be asked. She says taxpayers will not be paying for her trip. So who will? Was her trip funded by herself, Rinehart or One Nation and its members? If she was a guest of Rinehart, will the value of this gift be disclosed? Did anyone else fund flights and hotel rooms? Voters will make up their own minds about One Nation’s relationships with its wealthy patrons. Here are a few more. Does Hanson support her Senate colleague, Malcolm Roberts, when he says he has “respect” for Russian President Vladimir Putin? Does she support Roberts when he shares a notorious antisemitic illustration? And a few others. How can Australia cut net migration to 130,000 a year – yes, a target many want – without tanking economic growth? What police work will be set aside so officers have time to enforce a burka ban?



Some admire Hanson for the way she uses social media to bypass the mainstream and reach voters. Farage, speaking to this masthead at CPAC, said she was “very, very clever” on social media. CPAC was full of right-wing commentators talking about the decline of the mainstream media. Related Article Analysis

Pauline Hanson ‘We are a threat’: What leaked audio of Pauline Hanson at right-wing dinner reveals about her plans But if the mainstream media doesn’t matter, why does Hanson seem so paranoid about it? Could it be because coverage of her luxury holiday was everywhere over the past week – in print, online, on television, on radio? And the story bounced around Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and the rest? The old and new media fed off each other. This inflicted real brand damage on Hanson and One Nation, and that seems to be all her own fault. It told voters that she didn’t really want to take on the establishment – she wanted to join it in first class. Hanson, enjoying her recent rise in the opinion polls, seems to have a growing sense of her personal destiny. She told the CPAC audience One Nation could be in government after the next election.



But her address to the event did not draw a crowd. It was short and lacking in real power, even though she drew applause when she hit the usual conservative buttons (trans rights, net zero, white privilege, and so on). It was largely a repeat of her remarks at the dinner the previous evening, as if she could not find enough new things to say to fill two speaking slots. And her escape from the press seemed like the routine of a reclusive pop diva, not a serious politician. It was comic, but revealing. Tough politicians take questions. Weak ones run away. World.title: Manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate arrested in Miami
World.content:
Miami: Manosphere influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate have been arrested and detained in Miami, and British authorities will seek to extradite them to face charges for alleged sexual offences. Brady McCarron, a spokesperson for the US Marshals Service, said the warrant was sealed. However, the brothers are wanted in the United Kingdom, where they face rape and human trafficking charges. Andrew Tate, right, and his brother Tristan Tate at an Ultimate Fighting Championship match in Miami in April. Julia Demaree / AP British authorities have confirmed they will seek extradition for the brothers, who are dual US and British citizens. The former professional kickboxers promote hypermasculinity, unapologetic misogyny and a luxury lifestyle on social media, a niche known as the “manosphere”, and have millions of followers, mostly young men.



Related Article Analysis

Sexism Why some young men idolise Andrew Tate, and young women are disgusted In the UK, Bedfordshire Police said the brothers were detained after an investigation by police into a number of alleged sexual offences that resulted in additional charges. The Crown Prosecution Service has authorised 38 new charges against the brothers, bringing the total to 59. Andrew Tate, 39, faces 42 charges and Tristan, 38, faces 17. The original charges were based on a file of evidence submitted by officers from Bedfordshire Police into allegations dating back to 2012. Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit had continued to investigate reports of other alleged offences reported to both Bedfordshire Police and Hertfordshire Constabulary, leading to the additional charges, the police statement said. Assistant Chief Constable Karena Thomas said: “Officers from our major crime unit have been working closely alongside the Crown Prosecution Service and both national and international law enforcement agencies as part of this complex investigation.



“We understand the interest that this case will generate, but we would urge the public not to speculate and to allow the legal process to be carried out correctly. “There is no place for male violence against women and girls, and we will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us.” In the days before their arrest, the Tate brothers spent time in Washington DC, mixing with the city’s elite. They were hosted by US President Donald Trump’s “special envoy for global partnerships”, Paolo Zampolli, for at least one party. Zampolli confirmed to The Daily Mail that he hosted the brothers at a “summer gathering” for about 150 people at a home in Washington. The brothers were seen at Ned’s Club, a private members’ club near the White House frequented by senior members of the Trump administration. The Mail reported that some club members complained to management about their appearance.



Zampolli, who founded a modelling agency, introduced Trump to his now-wife Melania. He remains close to the president, and hosted meetings at Trump’s golf club in New Jersey on Saturday before the FIFA World Cup final. The Tate brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of sexual exploitation and human trafficking. They denied those allegations. The case did not go ahead because of procedural irregularities, and they moved back to the US in early 2025. World.title: When Hanson’s supporters examine all her policies, what they find could ‘horrify’ them
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPauline Hanson Opinion When Hanson’s supporters examine all her policies, what they find could ‘horrify’ them George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general July 19, 2026 — 1:53pm

July 19, 2026 — 1:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You have probably heard of “the Overton window”. It’s one of those faux-academic jargon phrases with which our language is increasingly cluttered. The eponymous window – named after the American social theorist Joseph Overton, who came up with the metaphor – defines the acceptable boundaries of public discussion. When those boundaries are exceeded, commonly by an iconoclastic politician who says something that no-one else has dared to say before, it is sometimes described as “shifting the Overton window”. One Nation leader Senator Pauline Hanson and One Nation Senator Malcolm Roberts at Parliament House. Alex Ellinghausen Nobody in our recent politics has shifted the Overton window more than Pauline Hanson. Her greatest impact has been in her assault on multiculturalism: what had been settled bipartisan policy for decades is now increasingly under challenge. For 30 years, Hanson has built her reputation as the plain-spoken Aussie who dares to say the unsayable. Even when so much of what she says is appalling, she has nevertheless thrived on the disdain of the political establishment. Its response to her unfiltered prejudices only reinforced her outsider status. As respect for that establishment eroded, she became the main beneficiary. That was not so much because of her ideas as her image: we love a fighter, the person who stands up to Canberra, and Pauline seemed to fit the bill perfectly. But in enshrining her as a kind of battlers’ Joan of Arc, her legions need to be careful what they wish for. When One Nation was a marginal presence, Hanson was easier to ignore. Today, when nearly one in three people tell pollsters she is their preference to be prime minister, the issues she raises dictate the parameters of much public debate. The Overton window has blown wide open.



Her popularity comes, however, at the cost of much greater scrutiny. It is that which may ultimately prove her undoing. Related Article Political leadership Pauline Hanson has momentum. Her biggest challenge is the company she keeps Hanson’s declaration that she could be prime minister changed the standard by which she is judged – for her admirers as much as by her critics. The question her supporters can no longer avoid is whether she is equal to the nation’s hardest job. Notwithstanding her outsider’s appeal, do they really believe that someone whose only demonstrated skill has been as a political stirrer really has what it takes to run the country? Of course, there will always be those members of the “plague on both your houses” crowd whose reaction will be: “Well, she couldn’t be any worse than what we’ve already got”. Actually, she could be. Viewing Hanson as an alternative prime minister has widened the scrutiny not just of her own capacities, but of her policies. Until now, it has been just a few of her unconventional pronouncements that got the public’s attention. Many of One Nation’s policies escaped attention, lost in the media frenzy around those utterances, together with the eye-catching stunts. No longer. As an aspirational party of government, attention will now focus on all of its policies. When that happens, even her devotees will have cause to think twice.



Obviously, there is the low-hanging fruit (pun intended) of people such as Malcolm Roberts. While all political parties have strange people in their ranks, this man would be a senior member of her cabinet. Do conservatives flirting with One Nation really want, sitting on the National Security Committee, a Putin-admiring man who promoted antisemitic material and appears more rabidly anti-American than the loopiest Green? Related Article Analysis

Pauline Hanson Hanson is sweating her five-star Euro summer more than she’s willing to let on Just as Senator Roberts’ unconventional foreign policy ideas have hitherto escaped notice – until revealed in this masthead last week – so too have many of One Nation’s other alarming policies. While many of Hanson’s headline-grabbing remarks may give her sympathisers a warm inner glow, once they start ferreting around in the One Nation policy cupboard, they will find much to horrify them. How many of Pauline’s blue-collar supporters will feel comfortable with her plan to make workers much easier to sack? How many of her libertarian sympathisers know about her plan to introduce a national identity card? How many of her admirers in rural Australia have thought about the consequences of her policy for the compulsory sale of foreign-owned agricultural holdings? This policy would force onto the market an estimated 14 per cent of Australian farmland, creating a massive glut which would immediately crash the value of every Australian rural property. Since those assets are commonly highly geared, the collapse in land values could put thousands of family farms into negative equity, potentially triggering the debt covenants in their mortgages. One Nation’s policy would be a calamity for rural Australia – yet I suspect few of Hanson’s admirers in country electorates are aware of it.



This is the “eternity of pain” of which Angus Taylor warned in his speech to the Sydney Institute on July 9 – pain which Hanson’s supporters would feel sooner and sharper than most other Australians. Taylor’s decision to muscle up to One Nation came later than it should have done but, for all the reasons I argued in this column recently, it was absolutely the right call. There can be no turning back from it now, however much some antic voices on the Liberal Party’s extreme fringes might object. The thing about Dr Overton’s window is that, however much it may shift, it never goes away. For the next two years, Pauline Hanson will be in the middle of the frame. George Brandis is a former high commissioner to the UK. He served as a Liberal senator and federal attorney-general. He is a professor at the ANU’s National Security College. World.title: Australian Opals coach suspended for ‘inappropriate comment’ to star player
World.content:
SportBasketballWNBA Australian Opals coach suspended for ‘inappropriate comment’ to star player Frances Howe July 19, 2026 — 1:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian coach Sandy Brondello has been given a one-game suspension for calling an opposing player a “protected species” during a game on Saturday (AEST). Brondello, 57, is head coach of the Opals – Australia’s women’s basketball team – and the Toronto Tempo, an expansion team in North America’s Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA). Sandy Brondello is head coach of the Australian Opals and the WNBA’s Toronto Tempo. Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The WNBA released a statement on Sunday morning (AEST) announcing that Brondello had been suspended without pay for one game for an “inappropriate comment” made about high-profile Atlanta Dream forward, Angel Reese. Brondello could be heard on the broadcast saying, “Angel, she’s a protected species” after a Tempo player, Nyara Sabally, was called for a defensive foul on Reese late in the game. Immediately after, Sabally was treated by the team’s medical staff for a rib injury and did not return to action. The Dream beat the Tempo 111-92.



The phrase “protected species” is often used in an Australian sporting context when referring to players who are thought to get preferential treatment from match officials. The comment was picked up by users on X after the game before Reese herself shared a post and tagged Brondello in it. The user had written, “Calling a black woman a species ...” To which Reese wrote, “Are we surprised!?” and added a clown emoji. Atlanta Dream’s Angel Reese shoots during a game against the Toronto Tempo in June. Getty Images Reese is one of the WNBA’s most recognisable players and is the current league leader in rebounds per game. Brondello responded with her own post, which read: “Angel, I’m sorry. Last night, in the emotion of the moment after Nyara’s injury, I used a phrase that I shouldn’t have used, and I take full responsibility for that. My frustration was with the officiating, but my words unfairly put the focus on you.



“I also understand that my words carried an impact beyond what I intended, particularly for Black women in our league, and I’m deeply sorry for that. I’ve spent my career competing with, coaching and learning from incredible Black women. “I regret that my words caused hurt to a community I respect so deeply. I have a lot of respect for you as both a player and a person, and I sincerely apologise to you, your teammates, and the Dream organisation for my comment.” View post on X The WNBA confirmed Brondello would serve the ban in the Tempo’s next match against the Las Vegas Aces on Tuesday (AEST) and added, “The WNBA expects all coaches and team personnel to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and respect that are fundamental to our league.” Brondello’s comment and ban have been made during a time of heightened concern in the league regarding the racial vilification of black players. The league’s commissioner Cathy Engelbert and its most high-profile player Caitlin Clark both made public statements earlier this month when Phoenix Mercury’s Alyssa Thomas was subjected to death threats and racial abuse online after she fouled Clark in a game on June 24.



A man was also fired from his job at a Hilton Hotel this week after calling Aces’ guard Chelsea Gray a racial slur over Instagram direct message. Related Article WNBA Why Serena Williams is this Australian’s new boss Reese did not reply to Brondello’s apology but shared another post which wrote “so many girls can learn from how [Reese] stands up for herself.” Three-time championship-winning college basketball coach and three-time Olympic gold medallist, Dawn Staley shared Brondello’s post and added “a real apology”. Brondello was announced as head coach of the Tempo for their inaugural season this year. She has coached in the WNBA since 2005 and was a player in the league before that. She is one of just two WNBA coaches to win championships with different teams and is the only Australian coach in the league.



During her time as a player for the Opals, Brondello competed at three Olympic Games – winning one bronze and two silver medals. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: The device detecting the world’s deadliest creature
World.content:
NationalNSWAI The device detecting the world’s deadliest creature Angus Dalton July 19, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To some, it’s just annoying, but to others, it marks the chilling call of the world’s deadliest creature: the buzz of a mosquito. In an effort to slash the extraordinary death toll wreaked by the insects, a University of Wollongong researcher has harnessed a super-efficient, lo-fi form of AI that can discern a disease-carrying mosquito from a harmless one by tuning in to this buzz. A low-powered AI device could help detect the world’s worst mosquito species. Michael Howard The detection device is one of a raft of new inventions using tiny machine learning, or TinyML, a low-power type of AI serving as the antithesis to the voracious large language models that require energy-guzzling data centres. First, Associate Professor Kiran Trivedi wanted to see if TinyML could identify the bird calls floating through his window.



Trivedi, a computer science expert from the university’s Indian campus in Ahmedabad, downloaded bird call data from Google and created a small model deployed onto a tiny chip that could identify the calls of species such as the Indian cuckoo. Once that was working, he turned to babies. Trivedi’s brother, a pediatrician who works in a neonatal ward, told him anxious new parents often brought in their infants to ask the doctor why they were crying. “So again, I collected the data for babies’ crying sounds, and created a model for that.” The result was another experimental device designed to deduce whether a baby was bawling because of hunger, sleepiness or discomfort.



“That is how it started,” Trivedi said. But crying babies, he thought, were hardly the world’s biggest problem. So he pivoted to mosquitoes, which kill 700,000 people per year via malaria, dengue and Zika. Each species has a unique wing beat. The malaria-carrying kind, Anopheles, has a low-pitched buzz. Culex mosquitoes carry Japanese encephalitis and Ross River virus; they buzz at medium pitch. Aedes aegypti, a dengue-carrying species also found in Australia, flies at the highest pitch. Associate Professor Kiran Trivedi at the UN’s AI for Good summit this week. UN AI for Good Trivedi used 40 gigabytes of mosquito sound data, equivalent to 10,000 stored photos, to make a model that was 150 megabytes – still too large for a small chip. To compress the model, he converted the audio recordings into images called “spectrograms”, which are visual representation of soundwaves. The AI learned to pick up patterns in the images invisible to the human eye.



Then, through a process called “quantisation”, he stripped back and simplified the model until only the information essential for making accurate predictions remained. The resulting model was a tiny 19 kilobytes, about the size of a five-page Word document. Associate Professor Kiran Trivedi’s lo-fi mosquito detection device. University of Wollongong “I deployed that onto my device, connected a display and some batteries, and it was, surprisingly, a perfectly working device.” He caught a mosquito in his room in Ahmedabad, in western India, and let it fly near the device. It was detected as an Anopheles mosquito; by far the deadliest species. The device is currently 88.3 per cent accurate.



This is TinyML at work, a form of AI that can operate off-grid, independently, on a tiny chip with little power. With the energy an LLM uses to generate a paragraph of text, a TinyML device can run for weeks. Related Article Data centres ‘More questions than answers’: Albanese’s data-centre vision risks renewables rollout “For AI, usually we need massive [amounts of] data, a powerful machine, and an internet network or Wi-Fi,” said Associate Professor Jianlong Zhou, an AI researcher at the University of Technology Sydney not involved in Trivedi’s research. “TinyML is different – we can use it in places with no power, no internet, no network. “TinyML collects data locally, processes it locally, and gives feedback locally, so there’s no privacy issues.” Zhou has researched TinyML applications in beekeeping, where TinyML nanosensors can monitor a hive’s environment down to humidity, CO2, pheromone imbalances in the queen bee, early chemical signs of Varroa mite infestations, and the vibrations of bees which signal an impending swarming event.



Smart agriculture, as well as wearable health sensors, will be major drivers of TinyML technology in the near future, he says. By one estimate, the number of TinyML devices in operation will spike to 2.5 billion by 2030. As for Trivedi’s device, he dreams the sensors could be mass-produced for 500 rupees, or about $7.50, and become part of a citywide detection network. A mock-up mosquito monitoring dashboard envisioned by Dr Kiran Trivedi, that could one day operate based on his devices. Dr Kiran Trivedi “It’s all about early detection,” he said. “Usually, what happens where I live is that you read in the newspaper that there are a lot of mosquitos breeding, and dengue has been found. But the outbreak has already happened and a lot of people have already been infected.” The technology he’s working on could catch mosquito outbreaks as they begin, leading to targeted early control measures such as insecticide fogging. He also imagines the model built into smart speakers such as Alexa and alerting people when a disease-causing mosquito is buzzing nearby.



Trivedi displayed his technology at the UN’s AI for Good summit this week. “If we can identify the mosquito species and help society, it could be a great success for me,” he said. World.title: This is what English football looks like when the pressure is off
World.content:
SportFIFA World Cup This is what English football looks like when the pressure is off Mike McGrath Updated July 19, 2026 — 1:46pm ,first published 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Miami: England played in the craziest match of the World Cup as they defeated France in a 10-goal thriller to win the bronze medal on Saturday (Sunday, AEST). At one stage, they looked like throwing away a four-goal lead at the Hard Rock Stadium, before seeing out a 6-4 win and securing their best finish at the tournament since winning in 1966. Jude Bellingham, Bukayo Saka and Reece James celebrate Saka’s hat-trick. Getty Images Here’s a look at the madness in Miami during the third-place play-off. Attacking intent



There were eyebrows raised when Declan Rice was selected despite his 68 previous games this season. He has described it as an “obscene” amount of matches but was called upon for one last effort and was charging forward in the first few minutes, intercepting a pass and curling into the bottom corner to kick off the scoring. But England were not done – there was no sitting back on their lead as they did against Argentina. England manager Thomas Tuchel’s attackers were pouring forward and getting behind the French defence with balls over the top. Ezri Konsa and Bukayo Saka (twice) were on the scoresheet by half-time. Loading The French not turning up As good as England were in that first 45 minutes, it was clear that France were already on the beach following their defeat by Spain in the semi-final earlier in the week. Players who were used to high-intensity pressing were allowing white shirts to walk past them with the ball.



By the break, Saka had run 1.4km more than Kylian Mbappe. This was Didier Deschamps’s final game in charge of Les Bleus, but players were treating it like an exhibition match. Flicks, tricks and no defending. The best half-time interview The half-time interview is another of FIFA’s new ideas. They have largely just been anodyne, aside from when Anthony Barry is in front of the camera. Tuchel’s assistant has been a breath of fresh air with his honesty and fought back the tears when analysing England’s first 45 minutes. “I am a little bit emotional, I can’t find the words to describe just how proud I am of these players,” said Barry. “They are playing a game out on the field with broken hearts, I see 11 lads out on the field with broken hearts, I’ve seen them in the hotel last few days – broken hearts.” Kylian Mbappe celebrates scoring his side’s third goal against England. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell



France go through the gears France decided to step it up after the half-time interval, with Deschamps calling for Ousmane Dembele and Bradley Barcola off the bench to lead their attack. Immediately, England were on the back foot despite being four goals up. Mbappe decided to show up too, pulling one back and celebrating with body language that suggested: we’re still in this. Barcola also found the net. This was Didier Deschamps’s final game in charge of Les Bleus, but players were treating it like an exhibition match. Mbappe takes command of Golden Boot race Mbappe’s double means he has overtaken Lionel Messi as the highest-scoring player in World Cup history, with 22. There is a question over whether goals in the third-placed play-off should count, but as it stands, they most certainly do. The Frenchman now has 10 at this tournament, two ahead of Messi – who plays in the final on Sunday.



It is the first time a player has reached double figures in one tournament since Gerd Müller for West Germany. Michael Olise set up his two goals and that made the former Crystal Palace midfielder the most creative World Cup player in the last 60 years with his seven assists. This is England’s best men’s World Cup since 1966. Getty Images England fail to learn lessons from semi-final ... This ended in victory for England, but there were red flags too with how France were allowed back in the game. Tuchel’s team dropped deep just like they did in Atlanta when they took the lead against Argentina. Tuchel says one of the big problems England face is how they play when the pressure is on. And once France started trying, they made England buckle again. ... but getting over the line



For the final 11 minutes, Tuchel called for his “starters” who had been rested on the bench. Jude Bellingham came on, to the delight of the neutral fans in attendance. Related Article FIFA World Cup Messi the link between Argentina and Spain’s colliding contrasts Elliot Anderson also came off the bench to try and keep the ball in central midfield, shifting the formation after England were in a 4-4-2. It was Djed Spence, one of England’s breakout stars of the tournament, who earned a penalty when the game was in the balance. Saka’s history-making hat-trick Bellingham has been “protecting the ball” for penalties, standing over the spot and holding the ball so opponents cannot get in the ear of England’s actual taker. He did this for Harry Kane earlier in the tournament. But with Kane rested, Saka completed his hat-trick from the penalty spot. The Arsenal forward was an unused sub against Argentina but made history with his hat-trick here, joining Geoff Hurst, Gary Lineker and Kane as England players with World Cup hat-tricks to their name.



Stoppage-time chaos Dembele set up a frantic final few minutes when he found the net, finishing off a counter-attack started by Dayot Upamecano. There was still time for Bellingham to round off his stunning cameo with a spectacular goal, running through the France defence and dummying the goalkeeper before finding the net. The Telegraph, London

World.title: Taranaki's St Andrew's Church scheduled for $4.2m restoration
World.content:
A Taranaki church built to remember the men from Inglewood who died during the First World War is scheduled for a $4.2 million restoration project.

In the 1920s when the people of the area wanted to create a memorial for the 138 local men killed during the conflict, they built a church and enshrined their names on a marble tablet on the wall.

More than a century on, the community is banding together again to preserve St Andrew's Church.

The Anglican church, which was completed in 1923, is a Schedule 1 protected building in New Plymouth District Council (NPDC)'s Part Operative District Plan and needs a new roof and earthquake-strengthening to see it through another century.

The Taranaki Anglican Trust Board (TATB) is set to start the $4.2m project with funding from residents and other donors, including $100,000 from the NPDC's Built Heritage Protection Fund.

St Andrew's Property and Admin Committee chair, Graeme Sykes, said the church was still seeking about $1m for the work, and pledges could be made at standrewsinglewood.org.nz.

"This is an important piece of our town's history, both as a memorial and as a distinctive architectural landmark. The parishioners at the time contributed to the construction of this church as a lasting memorial to those who gave their lives in the war, and now it's fallen to us to carry on this work and preserve it as a reminder of the tragic cost of war," said Sykes.

"We're very grateful to all the donors, including NPDC and the Lottery Environment and Heritage Fund, which has given $300,000. NPDC's a significant commitment and shows our district is serious about preserving our history."

The Built Heritage Protection Fund helps private property owners look after and preserve heritage buildings by funding work such as earthquake strengthening, repair or replacement of verandas or roofs, repiling, exterior cleaning and painting or specialist work like stonework.

"Heritage buildings are an important part of our historic legacy and they're part of the identity of our communities. By funding their preservation, we also support local jobs and businesses who do the work, helping to keep our district thriving and resilient and a place where people want to live, work and raise their families," said NPDC planning supervisor Lauren O'Byrne.

"As well as being symbolically significant, St Andrew's was exceptionally well designed and constructed with high-quality building materials and a number of distinctive features such as its bell tower, and the round arch windows and mouldings. The Italian marble war memorial dedication stone adds to its value for present and future generations."

Building owners could apply for funding from the Built Heritage Protection Fund until 21 August.
